title: Order of Operations and Calculating with Integers
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Number
summary: Work out calculations with brackets, powers and roots in the correct order, and estimate, multiply and divide positive and negative integers.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that brackets, indices (powers, square roots and cube roots) and the four operations are always worked out in a fixed order (8Ni.01)
Estimate, multiply and divide positive and negative integers, and find and explain general rules (generalisations) about the signs of the answers (8Ni.02)

blocks.text: Is 2 × 3^{2} equal to 36 or 18? Is (−6) × (−4) positive or negative? On this page you will learn the full **order of operations** for Stage 8 — now including powers and roots — and the rules for **multiplying and dividing negative numbers**, with quick ways to **estimate** answers so you can check your work. Everything on this page is Paper 1 (non-calculator) material, so practise it without a calculator.
Key words

items: integer
عدد صحيح — a whole number: positive, negative or zero (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …)
negative number
عدد سالب — a number less than zero, e.g. −7
index / power (plural: indices)
الأس — the small raised number: in 5^{3} the index is 3, so 5^{3} = 5 × 5 × 5
square root √
الجذر التربيعي — √49 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49
cube root ∛
الجذر التكعيبي — ∛64 = 4 because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64
product
حاصل الضرب — the answer to a multiplication
quotient
خارج القسمة — the answer to a division
estimate
تقدير — round the numbers to easy values, then calculate, to get an approximate answer
generalisation
تعميم — a rule that is true for a whole group of numbers, not just one example
inverse operation
العملية العكسية — the operation that undoes another: × and ÷ are inverses

blocks.text: 1. The order of operations — now with powers and roots
At Stage 8 the order of operations has **four levels**. Work from level 1 down to level 4. Inside one level, go from left to right.

items: **Brackets.** Work out everything inside brackets first. If there are brackets inside brackets, start with the innermost pair.
**Indices (powers and roots).** Work out squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots.
**Multiplication and division**, from left to right.
**Addition and subtraction**, from left to right.

rows: inside the bracket the power comes first: 8 − 8 = 0; then 5 × 0

blocks.text: Hidden brackets: root signs and fraction lines
Two symbols act **like brackets** even though you cannot see the brackets:

items: **A root sign covers everything under its line.** √(9 + 16) means: add first, 9 + 16 = 25, then √25 = **5**. This is **not** the same as √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7.

**A fraction line groups the top and the bottom.** In (12 + 8) ÷ (2 × 5), written as a fraction with 12 + 8 on top and 2 × 5 underneath, work out the top (20) and the bottom (10) first, then divide: 20 ÷ 10 = **2**.

blocks.title: −3^{2} is not the same as (−3)^{2}
blocks.text: In −3^{2} the power is done before the minus sign is applied, so −3^{2} = −(3 × 3) = **−9**. In (−3)^{2} the bracket tells you to square the negative number: (−3) × (−3) = **9**. A scientific calculator follows the same rule, so type the brackets when you mean (−3)^{2}.

blocks.title: BIDMAS and your calculator
blocks.text: Many books use BIDMAS (Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction). Remember that D and M have the same rank, and so do A and S — go left to right. A scientific calculator (allowed on Paper 2 only) follows the order of operations automatically, but only if you type the brackets you need. For a fraction such as (12 + 8) ÷ (2 × 5), type the brackets round the top and the bottom, or use the fraction key.

blocks.text: 2. Multiplying and dividing negative integers
**Multiplication is repeated addition.** 4 × (−3) means four lots of −3: start at 0 and make four jumps of −3. You land on **−12**.

blocks.text: **Fact families help with division.** Because (−6) × 4 = −24, you also know (−24) ÷ 4 = −6 and (−24) ÷ (−6) = 4. If you are unsure of a division, turn it into a multiplication: (−56) ÷ (−8) = ? asks "what times −8 makes −56?" The answer is **7**.
3. Generalisations about signs
Checkpoint likes to ask you to test a statement or explain a rule. These generalisations are always true:

items: **Same signs give a positive answer; different signs give a negative answer** (for × and ÷).

**Count the negative signs** when you multiply several numbers. An **even** number of negatives gives a **positive** answer; an **odd** number gives a **negative** answer. (−2) × (−3) × (−5) = 6 × (−5) = −30 (three negatives). (−1) × (−2) × (−3) × (−4) = 24 (four negatives).
**Multiplying by −1 changes the sign:** (−1) × 9 = −9 and (−1) × (−9) = 9.
**The square of any non-zero integer is positive**, because it is either positive × positive or negative × negative.
**Zero:** any number × 0 = 0, and 0 ÷ any non-zero number = 0. You can **never divide by zero**.
**If a × b is negative, exactly one of a and b is negative.** If a × b is positive (and not zero), a and b have the same sign.

blocks.text: To show a statement is **false**, one counter-example is enough (this is **convincing**). "The product of two integers is always bigger than both of them" is false: 5 × (−2) = −10, which is smaller than both 5 and −2.
4. Multiplying and dividing larger integers

items: **Decide the sign first** using the sign rules.
**Ignore the signs and calculate** with the positive numbers (grid method, column method or short division).
**Put the sign on the answer**, then check with an estimate.

blocks.text: **Example: (−23) × 14.** Different signs, so the answer is negative. Now work out 23 × 14 with a grid:
So (−23) × 14 = **−322**. Estimate to check: −20 × 15 = −300, which is close. ✓
**Example: 936 ÷ (−6).** Different signs, so negative. Short division: 9 ÷ 6 = 1 remainder 3; 33 ÷ 6 = 5 remainder 3; 36 ÷ 6 = 6. So 936 ÷ 6 = 156 and 936 ÷ (−6) = **−156**.
5. Estimating

To **estimate**, round each number to one significant figure (or to another easy number), work out the easy calculation, and keep the sign from the sign rules. Estimates are used to **check** answers and to answer "Which is the best estimate…?" questions. Show the rounded numbers — the examiner wants to see them.
Sometimes it is better to round to a number that divides easily rather than to exactly 1 significant figure. For 3 580 ÷ (−62), rounding to 3 600 ÷ (−60) gives a neat estimate of **−60**.
6. Putting it together: mixed calculations with negatives
Use the order of operations first, then the sign rules at each step. Remember that **subtracting a negative is the same as adding**: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Work out 4 + 3 × 2^{3}. [1 mark]

items: Power first: 2^{3} = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Multiply: 3 × 8 = 24.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** doing 4 + 3 = 7 first and getting 7 × 8 = 56, or working out 3 × 2 = 6 first and then 6^{3}.
**Worked example 2** — Work out (a) √(100 − 36) (b) 100 − √36. [2 marks]

items: (a) The root sign covers 100 − 36, so subtract first: 100 − 36 = 64. Then √64 = **8**.
(b) Only 36 is under the root sign: √36 = 6. Then 100 − 6 = **94**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** in (a), writing √100 − √36 = 10 − 6 = 4. You cannot take the root of each part separately.
**Worked example 3** — Work out (−6) × (−4) ÷ (−3). [1 mark]

items: × and ÷ have equal rank, so go left to right.
(−6) × (−4) = 24 (same signs → positive).
24 ÷ (−3) = −8 (different signs → negative). **Answer: −8**
Check by counting negatives: three negatives (odd) → negative answer ✓.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Kareem says, "When you multiply three negative numbers together, the answer is always positive." Is Kareem correct? Show how you know. [1 mark]

items: Test the statement with an example (specialising): (−1) × (−2) × (−3).
The answer is negative, so **Kareem is not correct**. Three is an odd number of negatives, so the product of three negative numbers is always negative.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** only writing "No". The mark is for the evidence — a correct counter-example or a correct reason.
**Worked example 5** — (a) Estimate (−412) × 29. Show your rounding. (b) Use your estimate to choose the exact answer: −1 948, −11 948, 11 948, −119 480. [2 marks]

items: (b) The answer must be negative and close to −12 000. Only **−11 948** fits.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** forgetting the negative sign in the estimate, or rounding 412 to 410 and 29 to 29 — that is not an estimate, it is still a hard calculation.
**Worked example 6** — Put **one** pair of brackets into this calculation to make it correct: 3 + 5^{2} − 4 × 2 = 56. [1 mark]

items: Without brackets: 3 + 25 − 8 = 20. We need a much bigger answer.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** putting the bracket round 3 + 5^{2}: (3 + 5^{2}) − 4 × 2 = 28 − 8 = 20. The bracket must make the square apply to 3 + 5.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Squaring before working out the bracket, or squaring only one number: 2 × 3^{2} = 18, but (2 × 3)^{2} = 36.
Splitting a root: √(9 + 16) = 5, not √9 + √16 = 7.
Writing −3^{2} = 9. Without brackets, −3^{2} = −9; only (−3)^{2} = 9.
Doing × before ÷ (or + before −) instead of going left to right: 24 ÷ 4 × 2 = 12, not 3.
Mixing up the rules for adding and multiplying negatives: (−5) + (−3) = −8, but (−5) × (−3) = +15.
Losing the sign in a long calculation. Decide the sign first and write it down before you calculate.
Rounding badly when estimating: round to 1 significant figure (or an easy number) and show the rounded numbers.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Work out" a mixed calculation with brackets, powers or roots — usually on Paper 1 (no calculator), worth [1] or [2].
"Insert brackets to make the calculation correct" — try the brackets that make one operation happen earlier, and check each try fully.
"Draw a ring around" the calculation with a given answer, or the best estimate.
"Is she correct? Explain your answer" — give a calculation as evidence, e.g. a counter-example. Words alone rarely earn the mark.
"Write the missing number": (−6) × ☐ = 42. Use the inverse: 42 ÷ (−6) = −7.
On Paper 2 you may use a calculator, but you must still type brackets correctly — and an estimate tells you if you made a typing slip.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Order of operations and integers practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, no calculator (Paper 1 style). Write your working on paper, type the final answer, then check the full solutions.

questions.e: Same signs give a positive answer. 7 × 8 = 56, so (−7) × (−8) = 56.

questions.q: Work out (−34) × 26 without a calculator. Show your working.
questions.e: Different signs, so the answer is negative. 34 × 26: 30 × 26 = 780 and 4 × 26 = 104; 780 + 104 = 884. Answer: −884. (Estimate: −30 × 30 = −900 ✓.) Mark scheme style: 1 mark for 884 seen, 1 mark for −884.
Left to right: (−2) × 5 = −10; (−10) × (−3) = 30; 30 × (−1) = −30. Check: three negative numbers (odd) → negative answer.

questions.q: Ahmed multiplies five negative integers together. Which statement is always true?
c: The answer can be positive or negative.
questions.e: Each pair of negatives multiplies to a positive. Five negatives = two pairs and one extra negative, so the product is always negative. An odd number of negative factors always gives a negative answer.

questions.q: a and b are both negative integers. Is a ÷ b positive or negative? Write positive or negative.
questions.e: a and b have the same sign (both negative), and same signs give a positive answer, e.g. (−12) ÷ (−3) = 4. So a ÷ b is positive.
Innermost bracket: 3 + 2 = 5. Power: 5^{2} = 25. Inside the outer bracket, divide before subtracting: 25 ÷ 5 = 5, then 18 − 5 = 13. Finally 2 × 13 = 26.
Roots and powers first: ∛125 = 5 (5 × 5 × 5 = 125) and 4^{2} = 16. Multiply: 5 × 2 = 10. Subtract: 10 − 16 = −6.

questions.q: Which is the best estimate of (−587) ÷ 31?
questions.e: Round: −587 ≈ −600 and 31 ≈ 30. (−600) ÷ 30 = −20. Different signs give a negative answer, so −20. (The exact value is about −18.9.)
Use the inverse operation: ☐ = 42 ÷ (−6) = −7. Check: (−6) × (−7) = 42 ✓ (same signs → positive).

questions.q: Mona says, "−3^{2} = 9." Explain Mona's mistake and write the correct value of −3^{2}.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explains that the power is worked out before the negative sign is applied / she has worked out (−3)^{2} instead / 3^{2} must be done first. 1 mark: −9 (cao). Do not accept just "she is wrong" without a reason.
questions.e: The index comes before the minus sign, so −3^{2} = −(3^{2}) = −(9) = −9. Mona worked out (−3) × (−3) = 9, which is (−3)^{2}, a different calculation with brackets.

questions.p: A submarine changes its depth by −45 metres every minute.
questions.q: Work out the total change in depth after 12 minutes. Give your answer as a negative number.
questions.e: Total change = 12 × (−45). 12 × 45 = 10 × 45 + 2 × 45 = 450 + 90 = 540. Different signs → negative, so the change is −540 m (the submarine goes 540 m deeper).

questions.q: Put one pair of brackets into this calculation to make it correct: 20 − 8 ÷ 2 + 2 × 3 = 12
questions.ms: 1 mark: (20 − 8) ÷ 2 + 2 × 3 = 12. No other position of one pair of brackets gives 12.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Order: Brackets → Indices (powers and roots) → × and ÷ left to right → + and − left to right.
A root sign and a fraction line act like brackets: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.
× and ÷: same signs → positive; different signs → negative. Count the negatives when you multiply several numbers.
For big numbers: decide the sign, calculate without signs, attach the sign, then check with an estimate (round to 1 significant figure).
